title: Comparing and choosing
job: More, less, better — stating a preference
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: -boda IS THE COMPARISON PARTICLE and the WORD ORDER is the delta. It attaches to the thing compared AGAINST, and that phrase comes in the MIDDLE, before the predicate: i-geo-ga geugeo-boda bissayo — literally "this, than-that, is-expensive". English puts the standard last ("more expensive than that") and Korean puts it where a verb-final language puts everything: in front of the verb. deo ("more") is optional and usually present, and it is M5's row doing its second job.

The superlative is gajang or jeil in front of the descriptive verb — gajang keoyo, jeil masisseoyo — with the group marked by jung-eseo, "among". Both words mean the SAME thing and jeil is the more colloquial. There is no distinction to invent between them.

NOTHING DECLINES AND NOTHING AGREES, which is the relief this course keeps offering and should keep naming: Korean's difficulty is in the particles and the endings, never in the shapes of its adjectives. A comparative is the plain descriptive verb with a particle somewhere else in the sentence.

THE TOPIC PARTICLE DOES ITS SECOND JOB HERE, and this is the module that finally explains M3's law: -eun/-neun marks CONTRAST, and a comparison is contrast. i-geo-neun bissayo, geugeo-neun ssayo — this one is expensive, that one is cheap. M3 taught the distinction as a rule; here a learner sees why it was worth the trouble, and no new particle is opened for it.

STATING A PREFERENCE: deo joahaeyo, "like more", on L1-M1's joahaeyo row. There is no separate verb for "prefer" — which is the mirror image of German's lieber, where an ADVERB carries what English gives to a verb, and worth naming as such. eoneu ("which") is the choosing word and a sibling of L1-M9's wae and L1-M8's myeot; -hago joins the two options.

sentences.cue: This one is more expensive than that one.

words.note: It sticks to what you are comparing AGAINST, and that phrase comes before the verb. English puts the standard last; Korean puts it in the middle.
The partner of L1-M1's i-geo: i-geo is near me, geugeo is near you. Both are written joined, because a bare demonstrative would collide with a particle's key.

sentences.trap: Nothing in bissayo changes for the comparison. The whole of it is carried by -boda sitting on the other thing, which is why Korean needs no comparative form at all.
sentences.sound: i-GEO-ga GEU-geo-bo-da bi-SSA-yo. -boda runs straight onto its noun with no pause.

variations.cue: That one is more expensive than this one.
This one is more expensive than that one.
variations.changed: with M5's deo, which is usual and optional

variations.cue: This one is expensive. That one is cheap.
variations.changed: the contrast done with M3's topic particle instead

mistake.why: The standard comes before the verb: I-geo-ga geugeo-boda bissayo.

sentences.usage: Comparing two things you can both see.
sentences.mnemonic: -boda sticks to the loser, and comes first.

words.note: The opposite of M5's deo, and it goes in the same slot, right in front of the verb. It is used far less often than deo — Korean prefers to say the other thing is more.

sentences.trap: geugeo-neun and not geugeo-ga, because a comparison IS a contrast. M3 taught the topic particle as a law; this is the sentence that shows what the law was for.
sentences.sound: GEU-geo-neun deol bi-SSA-yo. deol is one short syllable.

variations.changed: the same fact said the way Korean prefers

mistake.why: A comparison is a contrast, so it takes the topic particle: Geugeo-neun deol bissayo.

sentences.usage: Talking yourself into the cheaper one.
sentences.mnemonic: deo is more. deol is less. One letter.

words.note: It goes straight in front of the descriptive verb and changes nothing about it. jeil means exactly the same and is more colloquial.

sentences.trap: ppallayo is the same word it was in M4, unchanged. Korean builds a superlative by putting one word in front, and nothing in the adjective moves — which is what rule 2 keeps promising.
sentences.sound: ji-ha-CHEO-ri GA-jang ppal-LA-yo. gajang is two even syllables.

variations.changed: jeil, which means exactly the same

variations.cue: The subway is faster than the bus.
variations.changed: a comparison of two rather than a top of the list

mistake.why: gajang goes in front and nothing follows the verb: Jihacheol-i gajang ppallayo.

sentences.usage: Settling an argument about how to get there.
sentences.mnemonic: One word in front. Nothing else moves.

sentences.cue: Of all fruit, apples are the tastiest.

words.note: jung, 'the middle', with M4's -eseo. It marks the GROUP a superlative picks from, and it comes first because Korean puts the frame before the claim.
Fruit in general. L1-M8's sagwa is one of them, which is what makes this the natural group for a first superlative.
The same job as gajang and slightly more colloquial. There is nothing to choose between them beyond how the sentence sounds.

sentences.trap: The group comes FIRST, before the thing picked out of it. English says 'apples are the tastiest fruit' and Korean says 'among fruit, apples are tastiest', which is one more case of the frame preceding the claim.

variations.cue: Of all fruit, apples are the cheapest.

variations.changed: without the group, which is often obvious

mistake.why: The group goes in front: Gwail jung-eseo sagwa-ga jeil masisseoyo.

sentences.usage: Picking a favourite out of a named set.
sentences.mnemonic: Name the group, then pick from it.

words.note: It always stands in front of a noun and never alone — eoneu geo, eoneu yoil-i. A sibling of L1-M9's wae and L1-M8's myeot, and like them it takes no topic particle.
The bare 'thing' that L1-M1's i-geo already contains. In speech it shortens to geo, which is why eoneu geo-ga and not eoneu geot-i.

sentences.trap: deo joayo is Korean's whole comparative here — no second thing is named and none is needed, because the question itself supplies the set. English needs 'better than what?' and Korean does not.
sentences.sound: EO-neu GEO-ga deo JO-a-yo. eoneu is two light syllables.

variations.changed: joahaeyo, so the thing becomes an object

mistake.why: eoneu always stands in front of a noun: Eoneu geo-ga deo joayo?

sentences.usage: Asked while holding two of something.
sentences.mnemonic: eoneu never stands alone. It leans on a noun.

words.note: It joins two NOUNS and never two sentences — L1-M10's geurigo does that. The particle goes on the first one only, and the second takes the sentence's own particle.

sentences.trap: -hago sits on the FIRST noun, not between them as English's 'and' does. And the object particle goes on the second noun alone, because the pair behaves as one object.
sentences.sound: KEO-pi-ha-go CHA-reul jo-a-HAE-yo. hago runs straight onto keopi.

variations.display: Keopi-hago cha jung-eseo eoneu geo-ga joayo?
variations.script: 커피하고 차 중에서 어느 거가 좋아요?
variations.cue: Coffee or tea — which would you like?
variations.changed: the pair as a group to choose from

mistake.why: -hago goes on the first noun: Keopi-hago cha-reul joahaeyo.

sentences.usage: Answering what you drink, before the choosing starts.

words.note: A film and the cinema alike. yeonghwa bwayo, 'I watch films', uses M6's bwayo — the same verb as seeing anything else.

sentences.trap: THERE IS NO KOREAN VERB FOR 'PREFER'. deo joahaeyo — 'like more' — is the whole of it, which is the mirror image of German, where an adverb carries what English gives to a verb. Neither language is missing anything.
sentences.sound: YEONG-hwa-reul deo jo-a-HAE-yo. The h of joahaeyo is silent.

variations.changed: without deo, so no comparison at all

mistake.why: joahaeyo takes an object and joayo does not: Yeonghwa-reul deo joahaeyo.

sentences.usage: Answering a choice without refusing the other thing.

words.note: The opposite of L1-M9's manayo, and a descriptive verb like all of them. It covers both 'few' and 'little', because Korean does not count that distinction.

sentences.trap: Korean makes no difference between 'few' and 'little'. One word covers a countable shortage and an uncountable one, which is one distinction fewer than English asks a learner to keep.
sentences.sound: SI-ga-ni JEO-geo-yo. The n of sigan runs into the particle.

variations.changed: something countable, and the same word

mistake.why: Small in number is jeogeoyo, and it is a verb: Sigan-i jeogeoyo.

sentences.mnemonic: jagayo is small. jeogeoyo is few.

words.note: M3's ssayo in its modifier shape. A superlative in front of a noun is just jeil plus that shape, and nothing declines.

sentences.trap: jeil goes in front of the MODIFIER, not in front of the noun. jeil ssan geo, never ssan jeil geo — the whole superlative phrase builds leftward, as every Korean description does.
sentences.sound: JE-il ssan GEO-reul joo-SE-yo. The ss is tense.

mistake.why: jeil comes first: Jeil ssan geo-reul juseyo.

sentences.usage: In a shop, once you have decided how to decide.

words.note: It is ALREADY a modifier and has no -yo form at all: sae gabang, but never gabang-i saeyo. One of a handful of Korean words that only ever stand in front of a noun.

sentences.trap: sae cannot be a predicate. Every other describing word in this course is a verb first and a modifier second; sae is a modifier and nothing else, and saeyo does not exist.
sentences.sound: sae ga-BANG-i deo JO-a-yo. sae is one syllable, close to English 'say'.

variations.changed: asking for it, with M1's request

mistake.why: sae is only ever a modifier: Sae gabang-i deo joayo.

sentences.usage: Choosing between two of the same thing.
sentences.mnemonic: sae has no verb. It only leans on nouns.

comprehensionPool.cue: This one is more expensive than that one.
Of all fruit, apples are the tastiest.
This one is expensive. That one is cheap.
The subway is faster than the bus.
